results.comment: 15:40 The elevator sequence is damning for Oswald unless Givens's testimony was falsified. Lunch time, Oswald is on 5th floor, everyone sees him, he beckons them to shut the gate when they get off so he can use the elevator. This gives the impression he's coming to lunch as well. But Givens's unexpected trip to the 6th floor catches Oswald there. Givens even reports seeing him near the window where the shots were fired. So 5th floor Oswald was calling to his coworkers so he could ride up to the 6th floor, not down to lunch. Since both elevators had just descended, he could have easily just taken the stairs up one floor to the 6th, but instead he waited for the elevators to go all the way down, call for someone to shut the gate, and come all the way back up, all just to go from floors 5 to 6, at lunchtime. HIGHLY suspicious. Then Givens asks 6th floor Oswald if he's coming to lunch and STILL he says no, and again instructs Givens to close the gate when he's done using the elevator so it will come back up. It seems highly, highly likely that Oswald intended to shoot the President and then ride the elevator, which was already waiting for him, down to the 2nd floor and pretend to have been eating lunch the entire time.

results.comment: It's not that eyewitness testimony is useless... It's that some witnesses are drastically less useful than others in regards to their powers of observation and their individual susceptibility to their memories being manipulated either by their own minds or by various social pressures.  The guy at 1:08:27 is a fantastic example of someone who may not have the best powers of observation, but who did not yield to internal or external pressures when being questioned about something that they know they did not observe well.  Most people, when asked so many times about the package, would have begun filling in details about it, based on guesses from their memory. Most people want to be helpful and please the interviewer, whether they consciously recognize that or not, and would likely begin providing unreliable details, whether they consciously recognized what they were doing or not.  But not that dude. He tells them over, and over, and over that he didn't pay attention to it. And that's one aspect of accurate eyewitness testimony. Not just realizing what you saw, but recognizing what you didn't see.
results.comment_focus_summary: The commenter highlights an eyewitness (Wesley Frazier) repeatedly stating he 'didn't pay much attention to the package' and being resistant to filling in details under questioning — i.e., recognizing what he didn't observe.
